title: Water into wine (John 2:1–11)
hookLine: a wedding runs dry; Mary tells the servants to do whatever he says

cards: A cake collapses. A band doesn't show. Weddings go wrong.
Here's one in Cana, a village in Galilee. Jesus is there with his first disciples, and his mother too. In the middle of the feast, the wine runs out.
Historians of the period say that would have embarrassed the hosts badly, since a wedding feast put a family's hospitality on display. John doesn't explain any of that.
He says only that the wine ran short, and that the mother of Jesus spoke up.

teach.b: She goes to her son with four words: "They have no wine." Just the need, laid in front of him. His answer sounds sharp to our ears: "Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come."
But woman wasn't rude in his language; it was a respectful way to address someone, and he'll call her the same thing from the cross. Then Mary does something unexpected. She doesn't argue.

teach.h: WHATSOEVER HE SAITH UNTO YOU, DO IT.
teach.b: She tells the servants: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." Those are her last recorded words in John's Gospel. And John never gives her name; she's always the mother of Jesus.

teach.h: SIX STONE JARS, FILLED TO THE BRIM.
teach.b: Six stone water jars stand there, the kind used for washing by the rules of purity, each holding, the King James says, two or three firkins. That's a lot of water. Fill them, he says, and they fill them to the brim.
Now draw some out and take it to the head of the feast. It's wine.

The man in charge, not knowing where it came from, calls the bridegroom over, puzzled: everyone serves the good wine first, and the cheap stuff after people have had plenty, but "thou hast kept the good wine until now."
The King James calls it the beginning of miracles, but John's Greek word is semeion, a sign: something that points past itself.

teach.h: THOU HAST KEPT THE GOOD WINE UNTIL NOW.
teach.b: This is the first. Christians read Mary's part in different ways. Catholics and Orthodox Christians often see her here bringing people's needs to her son.
Many Protestants dwell on how she points away from herself: do whatever he tells you.

how: Many churches read the wedding at Cana at weddings and in the weeks after Epiphany, and Catholics pray it as the second luminous mystery of the rosary. Many Christians see in it a blessing on marriage and on ordinary celebrations.

o: a magic trick to impress a crowd
a sign that points past itself
a blessing spoken over a wedding

games.q: you're a servant at the wedding. a guest's mother says: whatever he tells you, do it. then he tells you to fill six huge washing jars with water. what do you do?
o: tell him it's wine you need, not water.
games.why: they fill them up to the brim. only when they draw it out and serve it does it turn out to be the best wine of the feast.

practice: Think of a celebration coming up or going on now, a birthday, a new baby, a friend's small win, a wedding, a holiday meal, and look at it the way Mary looked at the wedding: where is the wine running low, who's doing all the work, who's quietly worried it won't be enough?
Notice one place that needs a hand. If you pray, you can bring it to God in four words: they have no wine.

wordCard.voice: Semeion. John's Greek word for sign, something that points past itself, which is what he calls this first wonder at a wedding in Cana.

orig.note: Greek: a sign. John's word for the wonders Jesus does: things that point past themselves.

carryVoice: Your line: do whatever he tells you. Tomorrow, a woman at a well, at noon. Day fifty-two counts.
